opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think shared tools are really valuable, but with an important caveat. A lot of the most useful building blocks for agents are pretty universal. Almost every agent needs some way to read and write files, run code, search, or call out to an API, and it doesn't make sense for every team to reinvent those from scratch. Standardizing the interface, so a tool built once can plug into lots of different agents and applications, saves a ton of duplicated effort and lets the ecosystem compound.

The caveat is that what we've seen over and over is that the details of a tool matter enormously for how well a model can actually use it. We spend almost as much time on what I'd call the agent-computer interface as people spend on prompts. That means the tool's name, its description, the parameter formats, what the error messages say, how much output it returns. A generic tool that was designed for a human developer, or as a thin wrapper around an existing API, often isn't shaped the way a model wants to use it. So I'd encourage people to treat shared tools as a starting point, then actually look at transcripts of your agent using them and iterate. Put yourself in the model's shoes: if you only had this description and this docstring, would you know exactly how to use it?

My general advice is to start simple. Use the general-purpose pieces where they fit, keep the number of tools small, and only build something custom when you see the model consistently struggling with the generic version. The best agents I've seen aren't the ones with the most elaborate frameworks. They're the ones where someone really carefully thought through each tool from the model's perspective.

r001.rationale: The response recommends shared general-purpose tools as a starting point and custom tools when needed, but it does not express an expectation that AI agents’ ultimate end applications will be bespoke.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because when we were building out Claude Code internally, the big question was: how much of this should be bespoke tooling versus just giving the model the same general-purpose tools a human engineer would use?

And my honest take is that general-purpose tools win more often than people expect. The intuition a lot of people start with is that agents need special, agent-shaped interfaces — a custom API for everything, structured JSON in and out, a tool for every little action. And that's not totally wrong for narrow products. But the thing that surprised us is how much mileage you get from just giving a capable model a terminal, a file system, and the ability to run commands. Those tools weren't designed for AI, they were designed for humans, but they're incredibly composable and the model has seen millions of examples of people using them. So it already knows the idioms.

The other reason I like shared tools is that they're a kind of common ground. If my agent and your agent both speak bash and git and HTTP, they can interoperate without us having negotiated anything. That's really why something like MCP exists — it's trying to make the tool layer a shared thing rather than every agent builder reinventing a slightly different connector to Slack or GitHub or a database. The ecosystem gets way more value when a tool gets built once and every agent can pick it up.

Where I think you do want purpose-built stuff is at the edges: permissions, sandboxing, observability. A human using a terminal has judgment about what's dangerous. An agent needs that encoded somewhere, and the general tool doesn't give you that for free. So the pattern I'd recommend is general-purpose tools for capability, and a thin, deliberately designed layer around them for safety and control. Don't rebuild the tool — wrap it.

And the last thing I'd say is that as models get better, the argument for general tools gets stronger, not weaker. Every bespoke interface you build is a bet that the model can't figure out the general one. That bet keeps losing.

r001.rationale: The response says bespoke interfaces can suit narrow products and recommends purpose-built safety and control layers, but it does not express an expectation that AI agents’ ultimate end applications will be bespoke.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of value in giving agents the same general-purpose tools that people use. A computer, a terminal, a browser—those let you do an enormous range of things without someone having to build a special integration for every task.

But there’s a tradeoff. A purpose-built tool can make a particular action much easier and more reliable. If your agent needs to look up a customer record, you probably want to give it a straightforward way to do that, rather than make it navigate through five pages in a browser.

So I see those as complementary. General-purpose tools give you broad coverage, and specialized tools give you efficiency for the things you do frequently. For someone building an agent, the question is: where does the model actually need help? Start with a small set of useful tools, see where it struggles, and add structure there.

r001.rationale: The response says specialized tools can complement general-purpose tools, but it does not express an expectation that AI agents’ ultimate end applications will be bespoke.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a useful distinction between sharing the tools and sharing how an agent uses them. A lot of agents need the same basic capabilities: searching, reading files, running code, interacting with other systems. You don’t want every team to rebuild all of that.

But the right workflow depends on the application. What information does the agent need? When should it ask a person for help? What actions should it be allowed to take? A general-purpose tool doesn’t answer those questions for you.

So I’d like those tools to be reusable building blocks, with clear interfaces, and let people building agents compose them around their particular task. You get the benefit of shared infrastructure while still having control over the behavior that matters to your users.

r001.rationale: The response says agent workflows depend on the application and that builders should compose shared tools around their particular task, conveying that end applications will be bespoke.
